name: Canberra Times cryptic crossword, Saturday 28 June 1975

blocks.note: surface reading: shameful, bringing disgrace on someone
setter's reading: the apostrophe splits off dis-creditable, entries that are the opposite of credits in an account

explanation.surface: Someone faces shameful accusations formally recorded against them.
explanation.walkthrough: The stray apostrophe hints that the word should be read as 'dis-creditable': the opposite of credit in bookkeeping is a debit.
explanation.definitionFit: In accounting, sums entered against an account holder are the entries opposite to credits.

clue.text: Present with order last month, no local tax added

blocks.note: December, the year's final month, abbreviated
nought, zero
rates were the British local property tax

explanation.surface: Someone receives a medal in December, with no council tax charged on it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Order' looks like a command, but it is an order of chivalry, a medal.
explanation.definitionFit: To decorate someone is to confer an honour or medal on them, as when admitted to an order.

clue.text: A blessing when Jonson takes the stage

blocks.note: Ben Jonson, the Elizabethan playwright
when he takes the stage he is on

explanation.surface: Audiences feel blessed whenever the playwright appears in his own show.
explanation.definitionFit: A benison is an archaic word for a benediction or blessing.

blocks.note: first meaning: a score in rugby, made by grounding the ball
second meaning: setting something down, as an aircraft does on landing

explanation.surface: Someone is urged to attempt putting money into the bank.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Try' reads as 'attempt'; it is the rugby score, where the ball is grounded behind the line.
explanation.definitionFit: Grounding the ball over the line scores a try in rugby, and setting a plane down is landing.

clue.text: Tackle contentious item in medical language

definitions.text: Tackle contentious item in medical language

blocks.note: surface reading: deal with a disputed matter; setter's reading: tackle is collar (to grab someone) and a contentious item is a bone of contention
setter's reading: the everyday body part, given its anatomical name

explanation.surface: Someone is urged to address a disputed point written in doctors' jargon.
explanation.walkthrough: Collar plus bone gives collarbone, and the clue asks for the anatomists' Latin-derived term for it.
explanation.definitionFit: The collarbone's formal anatomical name, used by doctors, is the Latin-derived word for that shoulder bone.

clue.text: Sea cook pants over chopped liver

indicators.note: chopped food is cut up and mixed about, so these letters are scrambled

blocks.note: long johns are long underpants
taken as written

explanation.surface: A ship's cook gasps at the state of the chopped liver.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pants' looks like a verb (gasps), but it is underwear. Long John Silver is the one-legged ship's cook in Treasure Island.
explanation.definitionFit: Stevenson's pirate in Treasure Island signs on the Hispaniola as the ship's cook.

blocks.note: to vet is to examine closely
the usual abbreviation for central heating

explanation.surface: An engineer is told to inspect a building's boiler system.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plant' looks like machinery, but it is a living plant: vetch is a climbing legume.
explanation.definitionFit: Vetch is a climbing leguminous herb grown for fodder, a member of the pea family.

clue.text: Players without a point — a rummy sort of game

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside, so one part wraps round the other

blocks.note: the actors in a play
taken as written
north, a point of the compass
taken as written

explanation.surface: Players without a point to their game call it a rum one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' means outside here: the actors go round the first two letters, then the final A follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Canasta is a card game of the rummy family, played with two packs and melding sets.

blocks.note: surface reading: go off in the Roman fashion, like French leave
setter's reading: the Latin stage direction telling several actors to leave

explanation.walkthrough: French leave is departing without notice; the Latin-speaking version is the stage direction meaning 'they go out'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin stage direction meaning 'they go out' marks several actors leaving the stage together.

clue.text: Return principally reckoned as mere curiosity

blocks.note: first meaning: a yield calculated on the principal alone
second meaning: nothing more than plain inquisitiveness

explanation.walkthrough: 'Principally' looks like 'mainly', but it means on the principal, the original sum lent.
explanation.definitionFit: Banking's term for a return computed only on the original sum, not on earlier earnings; also, plain curiosity.

blocks.note: to con is to study or pore over
a joining together of things

explanation.surface: Merging study departments has left everything in chaos.
explanation.definitionFit: Disorder and muddle are synonyms for a state where nothing is in its proper place.

blocks.note: first meaning: a verb form, the present being one example
second meaning: taut, anxious

explanation.surface: Someone is there in person but visibly stressed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Present' reads as 'in attendance'; it is really the grammatical present, one of the verb forms.
explanation.definitionFit: Grammar's present, past and future are verb forms; the adjective also describes stretched nerves or muscles.

clue.text: Fruit of Miss Aylmer's cheerful beginning

blocks.note: Rose Aylmer is the subject of a famous short poem by Walter Savage Landor
the opening of the cheer 'hip, hip, hooray'

explanation.surface: It sounds like asking what came of a Miss Aylmer's happy start in life.
explanation.definitionFit: The red fleshy seed pod left on a rose bush after flowering is a fruit, used for syrups.

clue.text: There's a great life for the London author

definitions.text: There's a great life for the London author

blocks.note: surface reading: an exclamation about good living; setter's reading: Boswell's famous Life, the great biography of its subject
setter's reading: the man who wrote the poem London, not just a writer from the city

explanation.surface: A cheerful remark that the capital is a fine place for a writer to live.
explanation.walkthrough: Samuel Johnson wrote the poem 'London' (1738), and Boswell's Life of Samuel Johnson is the most celebrated English biography.
explanation.definitionFit: Samuel Johnson wrote the satirical poem London and was the subject of Boswell's celebrated biography.

blocks.note: to tan someone's hide is to beat them
go means vigour, drive

explanation.surface: A dance's rhythm is full of energy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beat' looks like the dance's rhythm, but it is the verb, to thrash.
explanation.definitionFit: A ballroom dance of Argentine origin, with sharp, gliding steps.

clue.text: Heavenly, England's first meeting with the Madrid team

indicators.note: first asks only for the opening letter of the country's name

blocks.note: the opening letter of England
taken as written
Real Madrid, the Spanish football club

explanation.surface: A football fan rhapsodises about England's opening match against Real Madrid.
explanation.definitionFit: Ethereal means delicate and otherworldly, as if belonging to the heavens rather than earth.

blocks.note: surface reading: a player who goes round the course
setter's reading: a tradesman who calls at houses on a regular route

explanation.surface: A golfer who reliably plays well under pressure.
explanation.walkthrough: A golfer plays rounds; the word is really a delivery man who does a regular route, like a milkman.
explanation.definitionFit: A tradesman's employee who makes regular delivery calls on a circuit of customers' houses.

clue.text: Repeated sporting engagement to perform in woodwind section

definitions.note: describes a match played again; the answer is the past participle

indicators.note: in places one part inside the other

blocks.note: the reeds are the woodwind section of an orchestra
to act or make music

explanation.surface: A rematch is arranged for the clarinettists and oboists.
explanation.definitionFit: A drawn cup tie is played again, so a repeated fixture is one that has been replayed.

indicators.note: something poor is in bad shape, so these letters are knocked out of order

blocks.note: taken as written, the apostrophe ignored

explanation.surface: Poor Ann has her own word for the scraps after dinner.
explanation.definitionFit: Remnants are the small pieces left over once the main part is used up, as scraps are.

indicators.note: some means only part of the following words is wanted

blocks.note: letters running across the words

explanation.surface: A patient worries about a chest ailment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chest complaint' looks like the definition; only 'complaint' is, and the chest supplies the last letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A complaint is an illness or ailment, and a pain in the ear is one such ailment.

clue.text: Treatment that puts years on us

blocks.note: taken as written
an age is a long span of years

explanation.surface: Some kind of handling has aged us prematurely.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Puts years on us' means the years go on, after, the word us.
explanation.definitionFit: Usage is the way something is handled or treated, as in rough usage.

clue.text: Assert sun rises from the lower regions

indicators.note: in a down entry, rising means reading upwards, so the word runs backwards

blocks.note: to aver is to declare
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone claims the sun comes up out of the underworld.
explanation.walkthrough: Avernus, a crater lake near Naples, was held by the Romans to be the entrance to the underworld.
explanation.definitionFit: Roman poets used the name of the lake at the gate of Hades for the underworld itself.

indicators.note: with no tail, the word loses its final letter

blocks.note: a kind or type

explanation.surface: A coin with no tails side would be a strange one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tail-less' teases the tails side of a coin; it means the word for sort loses its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Specie is money in coin form rather than paper notes.

blocks.note: pi is short for pious, sanctimonious
a rogue is a rascal

explanation.surface: It seems to describe the cunning of a hypocritical villain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Craft' suggests cunning, but it is a boat: a pirogue is a dugout canoe.
explanation.definitionFit: A pirogue is a dugout canoe, and a boat of any kind is called a craft.

blocks.note: surface reading: any writer of history; setter's reading: a particular Victorian historian, author of A Short History of the English People
setter's reading: put the word away after the historian's surname and it becomes the surname of Kate the Victorian children's illustrator

explanation.surface: A historian has run off with a woman called Kate.
explanation.walkthrough: Kate Greenaway illustrated Victorian children's books; her surname splits into the historian plus 'away'.
explanation.definitionFit: John Richard Green was a Victorian historian, author of A Short History of the English People.

indicators.note: turns suggests these letters are spun around into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written; LL.D. is a Doctor of Laws

explanation.surface: A lazy Doctor of Laws switches careers to compiling dictionaries.
explanation.walkthrough: Henry Liddell compiled, with Robert Scott, the standard Greek-English Lexicon.
explanation.definitionFit: Henry Liddell co-wrote Liddell and Scott's Greek-English Lexicon, so he was a dictionary compiler.

clue.text: The age of the single seater

blocks.note: first meaning: a long period, an era
second meaning: a bike, which carries one rider

explanation.surface: It reads like a history of the one-seat vehicle's era.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both a vast span of time and a bicycle, a pedal machine with one saddle.

clue.text: A pound for a pound of smooth dough?

blocks.note: level, flat
dough is slang for cash

explanation.surface: A baker weighs out smooth dough a pound at a time.
explanation.walkthrough: In betting, a pound staked to win a pound is odds of evens.
explanation.definitionFit: Betting odds at which the winnings equal the stake are called evens, a pound won per pound staked.

blocks.note: a line with a word missing
the source: Andrew Marvell's poem To His Coy Mistress

explanation.walkthrough: The line runs 'Yonder all before us lie / Deserts of vast eternity'; the answer is the missing word.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word in Marvell's line names the endless time stretching before the lovers after death.

blocks.note: first meaning: unfamiliar with
second meaning: in mint condition, never handled

explanation.surface: Someone has never acquired a taste for the herb.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mint' reads as the herb, but it is the collectors' sense: pristine, never used.
explanation.definitionFit: One meaning is unfamiliar with something; the other is new and never handled, as a mint stamp is.
